# Copper November 2011 

- After collapsing in September and then enjoying an impressive recovery at the end of October, price movements over the past month have resembled more of a controlled bloodletting than the haemorrhaging of two months ago.  Even though price fluctuations have not been as dramatic as the prior couple of months, they have, however, been characterised by a general downward trend as cash quotes dipped lower. 

- We have cut both supply and demand side estimates for 2011, with the net result that our expectation of a deficit this year not only remains intact but has increased from the prior month to -278kt, although we have lowered our 2011 price estimate owing to a weaker sentiment in the final quarter.  Our price forecast for 2012 is also lower at $8488/t, again a knock-on from the results of weak trading conditions in Q4 this year, with prices seemingly set to peak at $8900/t in the second quarter, fueled by an anticipated strong pick up in Chinese demand in tandem with a meaningful easing of credit restrictions across key consuming sectors. 

- The onset of cold rather than cool weather in much of the northern hemisphere is resulting in consumers keeping their hands in their pockets to stay warm, but negative economic sentiment is giving shoppers little cause to take them out to spend cash.  The same is true of demand conditions for copper, with the whole supply chain taking a wait and see attitude that is resulting in demand slowing appreciably.  As a result of the weaker-than-expected activity in the final part of the year we have lowered our demand growth estimate for 2011 to 3.8%, while we have also toned down projections for 2012, with a similar expansion of c.4% now expected. 

- It was Freeport who started the ball rolling in this current copper concentrate Mating Season by fixing terms with a Chinese smelter, widely rumoured to be Jiangxi Copper, at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb and a roll over of all other contractual terms.  Our feeling is that these TC/RCs will be accepted ‘as is’ by most market players or, alternatively, as has happened in the past, some miners will achieve lower effective settlement terms through pricing at this level but on a reduced tonnage (e.g. 80-85%) and then valuing the residual material on a spot basis.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Bloodletting slows to a drip** After collapsing in September and then enjoying an impressive recovery at the end of October, price movements over the past month have resembled more of a controlled blood letting than the haemorrhaging of two months ago.  Even though price fluctuations have not been as dramatic as the prior couple of months, they have, however, been characterised by a general downward trend as cash quotes dipped lower. 

Any momentum from the end of October rally had already run out of steam by the start of this month as relief from yet another final resolution to European debt problems turned to the more pragmatic realisation that there was probably more to come.  Indeed, after far too many months centred on Greece’s problems, the puns should have turned from tragedy to opera as the focus switched to Italy, but instead Prime Minister Berlusconi mirrored Brutus by falling on his sword to keep the tragic theme alive.  Having closed October at just under the $8000/t level, prices ebbed lower through the start of November, and had lost over $500/t by the 10<sup>th</sup> .  The formation of unity governments in both Italy and Greece did provide at least some relief, with cash quotes climbing by almost 4% in two days to touch $7709.25/t on the 14th.  But this respite was only brief, with prices continuing to edge lower again thereafter, until another uptick on the 28<sup>th</sup> , initially in response to a report that the IMF was preparing a rescue plan for Italy that was later denied.  The absence of any concrete solution to the euro zone debt crisis means that copper and other commodities are unlikely to garner any meaningful upside price traction, with the next wave of investor selling waiting in the wings to quell any meaningful support. 

**Codelco annual premia set lower** The relative weakness of demand across the globe has resulted in Codelco’s contract premia moving lower for 2012 in comparison with last year.  The key areas of Japan, China and Western Europe have all seen a decline, with these reflecting expectations of sluggish, or at least lacklustre demand.  Of all the regions, Western Europe has been granted the biggest discount, with premia down to $90/t from $98/t in 2011, which fits neatly with our view of no growth in regional demand next year.  We are much more sanguine on the outlook for Japan and China in 2012, however, with both of these countries set to enjoy a lower premia in 2012 - Japan down from $98/t to $93/t and China from $115/t to $110/t.  Although we forecast a recovery in growth in Japan next year and a similar rate of expansion to this year in China, clearly, the risks are weighted to the downside for both of these countries given their exposure to the West through exports.

**Chinese imports climb despite slowdown in underlying demand** Chinese cathode imports have maintained their recent impressive pace, climbing both on the prior month and particularly sharply on the same month a year ago. Indeed, cathode receipts were up by an impressive 74% year on year in October having reached 295kt, comfortably their highest level this year, although the growth rate was flattered a little by weak figures for October 2010. However, it is important not to misrepresent the strong growth in imports for robust Chinese demand. Key end use sectors are slowing appreciably as we move towards year end and although the tightness in the scrap market is favouring cathode use and as such better refined copper demand, underlying demand is certainly softening. The fundamental reason for the healthy imports is in part a combination of restocking at what are now relatively attractive prices but more so by firms using copper as collateral for financing reasons. As a result, spot premia have remained relatively elevated at around $110140/t. **European and US premia slide lower** Although demand for imported material has maintained the strength of premia in the Chinese market, the same cannot be said in Europe, where they have edged lower amid deteriorating conditions. The wait and see attitude that negative economic headlines have created has been amplified by eagerness to trim inventories in any case ahead of financial year-ends to shore up balance sheets and leave participants in the supply chain in destocking mode. As such, European cathode premia have dipped to the $35-55/t range. Meanwhile in the US, premia have remained around the 4.5-5.0c/lb mark, although we are hearing of higher numbers than this in the north east of the country as surging transport costs add to the delivery charges on the red metal. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 200 W Europe Shanghai US c/lb 10

**Stocks move lower towards year end** The decline in LME stocks over the past few months had primarily been led by withdrawals from Asian warehouses and while material continues to be shipped from these locations, Europe has also weighed in this month with withdrawals of its own. At the time of writing, LME stocks stand at c.393kt; lows not seen since the end of January and having lost c.80kt in the last two months alone. With premia so attractive in China, this has resulted in excess production being shipped out of Europe, with the result that demand for spot material in Europe has triggered a drawdown of residual European stocks. In tandem with the LME, SHFE stocks have also declined from 73.8kt at the end of October to 65.2kt. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2011 Page 3 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Disruptions strike out past 5% allowance** As with the previous month, ongoing strikes at Freeport’s operations at Grasberg in Indonesia (and Cerro Verde in Peru) failed to provide any meaningful support to prices, with the focus instead being on the debt crisis, whether that be in Europe or over concerns that US policymakers would fail to agree on plans to cut into their own deficit (which, unsurprisingly, they did towards the end of the month). One of the few areas of fundamental support for the market at present can be found in the level of mine disruptions thus far in 2011. At the start of each year we assume that 5% of our initial mine production capability forecast will be lost to disruptions of some sort, with even this allowance now looking less and less conservative. The data on disruptions is principally year to date, although the implicit assumption on Freeport is that Grasberg remains down during the first three weeks of December because even if the strike ended by the end of this month the pipeline still needs to be repaired, mining and milling restarted, concentrates slurry passed down the pipelines to be dried at port which will take several weeks. Indeed, so far this year, we have already exceeded the 5% disruption target and are now at 5.8% with December still to come, although interestingly, strikes have not been the largest single contributor to these losses, and in fact languish in fourth place behind technical problems, slow project ramp ups and low ore grades. Strike-related output losses at Cerro Verde, for example, have been kept to a minimum for reasons we have outlined in prior reports. In any case, as we note in our production section, this strike has now come to an end. **2012 price forecast tempered by demand concerns** We have cut both supply and demand estimates for 2011, with the net result that our expectation of a deficit this year not only remains in

tact but has increased from the prior month to - 278kt, although we have lowered our 2011 price estimate owing to the weaker sentiment that continues to prevail in this final quarter. The same is true of demand conditions for copper, with the whole supply chain taking a wait and see attitude that is resulting in demand slowing appreciably. As a result of the weaker-than-expected activity in the final part of the year we have lowered our demand growth estimate for 2011 to 3.8%, while we have also toned down projections for 2012, with a similar expansion of c.4% now expected. ### **Europe and CIS** **Economic data now mirroring dour sentiment** Last month when we discussed the divergence between economic activity and sentiment indicators we noted that the two would have to come into line with each other at some point. The 2% month-on-month fall in September’s eurozone IP suggests that economic activity is now catching up (or rather slowing down) with negative survey

data.  Of greater concern, among the data was that industrial powerhouse Germany was responsible for a major part of the fall.  Although our economic forecasts currently do not call for a double-dip recession, clearly the risks of this happening are now heightened.  Even without a further contraction in economic activity, we expect next year to be sluggish at best. 

**Semis output skating on thin ice** End users in the European market continue to maintain a cautious tone to their orders at semis producers, with the tumultuous economic backdrop creating something of a wait and see attitude to new business.  That we are now heading into the year end is of course making the situation a little worse, however, as firms would typically be looking to draw down stocks in any case.  As such, these two factors are combining to result in significant year-on-year contraction in output at some semis producers.  Although some producers do not feel that economic developments are the same as the end of 2008 when industrial activity did grind to a halt but without a line being drawn under the European debt crisis once and for all, the similarities may increase.  Indeed, without a clear resolution, the current caution could turn into paralysis which then would feed into a collapse in industrial activity and a sharp contraction in copper demand. 

**Aurubis closing down Swedish plant** Following on from its purchase of Luvata, Aurubis has decided to streamline its rolled copper operations as a result of structural over capacity in the industry.  As a result of this decision, the Finspang, Sweden, plant will be closed, with production likely to be moved to the Zutphen mill in the Netherlands and possibly Buffalo in the US.  Operations are due to wind down within a couple of years, with the net result being the loss of around 35kt of downstream capacity. 

**Aurubis withdraws from solar business** Meanwhile, Aurubis has decided to close its solar cell business amid strong competition and declining prices.  CIS Solartechnik, a joint venture with Cordes & Graefe, will close down by the end of this year as the scale of the business is no longer economically viable following fierce competition that has brought down prices and as such, margins.  We mentioned last month that the outlook for demand from the renewables sector had been tempered but this was related to uncertainty over investment in wind farms in particular.  The massive expansion of the use of solar has resulted in a proliferation of small companies and clearly, consolidation is required in the sector. However, this is not necessarily bad for demand for copper from the solar sector as fewer but bigger and healthier firms will likely continue to consume significant volumes of copper.  Indeed, there is still plenty of scope for further investment in solar farms in southern Europe in particular. 

**Construction activity looks set for contraction** The Euro construction orders PMI continues to hover around the

45 level, suggesting that construction volumes will continue to decline into the new year. The data showed declining activity in all of the residential, commercial and civil sectors, but there was a sharp deterioration in the commercial activity index in October, indicating that businesses are increasingly reluctant to invest in the current economic climate. In all, total construction is more than likely to contract in 2011 and 2012 pointing to weakness in copper demand from this sector. **Auto sector moves into slow lane** It now looks as though the previously strong automotive sector is also starting to feel the early signs of slowdown, with output in the key German market now falling on a year-on-year basis, although it must be noted that production was particularly strong in the final part of the year in Germany in 2010. Clearly, in times of economic uncertainty big ticket purchases such as cars slow sharply and so the outlook for 2012 ought to be somewhat muted based on our cautious view of economic activity in Europe next year. **European premia slip lower** The slowdown in orders at semis producers has unsurprisingly fed through into weaker cathode purchases and this has been reflected in a decline in premia in Europe. Premia now stand at around $35-55/t and when compared to much more favourable terms to ship to China, firms are choosing to opportunistically sell into the Chinese market given the current appetite there for imported material. **Q4 slowdown drags European demand lower** As a result of a sharper than previously expected slowdown in fourth quarter activity we have lowered our full year forecast for western European copper demand. We now expect a full year contraction of 2-3% in 2011, with little or no growth the following year. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2011 Page 5 of 21 Copper Monthly Update ### **Americas** **US rod markets remain under pressure** Despite slight amendments to summer months data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS) which generally increased shipments and production of copper rod for the months of July and August, September’s preliminary figures look like extending the mediocre business conditions which set in back in November three years ago. Since that fateful quarter, through to the end of Q2 this year, the average quarterly rod production from the US has been 305.5kt; Q3 2011’s output was 311kt, which continues to underline the fact that if the construction sector is not operating anywhere near passable levels, copper rod business will suffer. This is a far cry from the c.430kt average quarterly rod production levels that were in evidence since the start of 2000. #### **US production and shipments of wire rod – (kt)** 150

**Russian exports pick up again in September** As if lacklustre output and domestic shipments conditions were not enough, the sector is also having to contend with strong imports of Russian rod, even if it is not a simple task to see where, exactly, this Russian rod is making an impact. Since May, imports of rod from Russia have amounted to 23.8kt (5.8kt in September alone), and while this remains a small proportion (<2.5%) of production from domestic suppliers, it is still a challenge to compete against it when home consumer markets are slow. Russian rod entered US ports in significant volumes during 2003-2007, with upwards of 100kt coming in during 2005 and 2006. But this was at a time of much stronger markets, with Nexans from its Montreal rod mill also being able to participate in US construction growth by double the volume that it is exporting today. 2011’s US market scenario is very different, and the threat of continued import growth at the expense of domestic shipments will likely attract lobbyist attention in DC. **Auto sector remains “strong” point in copper demand** If construction shows little sign of life, the auto sector has managed to bounce back somewhat from its 2009 nadir. Then, we saw car and commercial vehicle production hit a low of 5.73M units, down from 8.7M the previous year. Despite all the negative sentiment over the condition of the US economy, auto production picked up to 7.76M units last year, and looks on track to recover 2008’s level in 2011. Indeed, production increased by 15% year-on-year in October to an annualised rate of 9.3M vehicles (seasonally adjusted), up 20% from June. For the year to date, production has increased by 9.1%. Further gains seem likely though the remainder of Q4, as producers continue to rebuild inventories after a 21% fall from March to July. We expect solid gains in auto production to continue into 2012, fuelled by pent-up demand. Meanwhile, total vehicle sales increased by 8% y- o-y in October and are now running above 13M units on an annualised basis. The main reason that US car demand growth has been so strong, despite poor macro-economic conditions, is that the level of sales is still unsustainably low. That is, consumers delayed purchases during the recession in 2008 and 2009, but that has resulted in a significant ageing of the US car fleet and now the many older vehicles need to be replaced. This replacement demand is expected to fuel 10%+ growth in sales in 2012. **Patriarch Partners takes Hussey Copper in auction** Private Equity firm Patriarch Partners, based in New York City, outbid a handful of other interested parties mid-November to gain the assets of bankrupt Hussey Copper Ltd., of Leetsdale, PA. Libertas Copper LLC, one of several subsidiaries of parent company Patriach, paid US$107.75M for Hussey, beating out competitors Revere Copper Products and private fund KPS Capital Partners LP (which last month bought TX-based r

od mill United Copper Industries from Mexico’s IUSA), and KHC Acquisition LLC of Red Bank, NJ. KHC was going to become the default owner of Hussey if no further interest was forthcoming.  Patriarch Partners LLC manages upwards of 75 companies across 14 industry sectors spanning manufacturing to cosmetics products and interior design, and specialises in turning around distressed entities.

### **China** 

**Cool running for industrial activity and prices** The slowdown in both industrial activity and, significantly, in inflation has continued, with latest data for both series revealing a further cooling in growth numbers.  Industrial production rose by 13.2% year on year in October, a modest slowdown compared to the 13.8% growth recorded in September but still a very robust rate of expansion.  The figure was very much in line with expectations, and further slowing is likely due to sluggish exports to Europe and the bite of previous monetary tightening.  Indeed, prior tightening appears to be bearing fruit, with growth consumer prices softening to 5.5% in October from 6.5% as recently as July.  That inflation is coming down, in addition to the weakness of key export markets, does afford scope for more accommodative monetary policy in the months to come and we are already hearing rumours that this may be about to happen. 

**Mixed picture for Chinese demand** The current picture of Chinese demand is somewhat mixed, with key consuming sectors seemingly veering off in opposite directions.  Wire rod has seen a significant improvement from mid-October onwards, but tube makers are suffering from the seasonal weakness of the air conditioner market.  Across a range of end use markets demand and output is slowing, with semis production mirroring this, however, the relative tightness in the scrap market is resulting in less direct use of scrap and favouring cathode consumption.  As such, this is tempering the slowdown in refined copper demand, but does not impact our full year demand forecast, which we maintain at 8% for 2011 and next year, although much of 2012’s growth will be in the second half of the year. 

**Wire rod takes the lead** It has been the tube market that has taken most of the plaudits this year in what has been a relatively tame year for demand by Chinese standards, however, it would seem that wire rod is now taking up the slack. It is noteworthy that in line with the upturn that we have noticed since the middle of October, there has been an improvement in investment overall and in the power grid in particular.  Investment in power generation and the grid increased by 6% and 3.6% month on month respectively, while in the first ten months of the year, investment is up by 2.7% and 14.4%.  Given that investment in the grid is much more copper intensive than in power generation the stronger year-to-date figures favour improving cathode demand.  In a

ddition, No.1 scrap has continued to trade at a premium to the Shanghai cash price, although the level of the premium has reduced from the range of RMB800-1,200/t in October to RMB136-600/t in November. With the high cost of No. 1 scrap, many up-casting wire rod mills fed by scrap have either cut their production or used more copper cathode, which encouraged both the production of major wire rod mills and refined copper demand. **ACR tube makers feel the chill** On a less positive note, however, tube makers are currently cutting back production sharply following the breakneck pace of production earlier in the year. The high level of stocks of air conditioners and the seasonal slowdown has forced ACR tube makers to trim output aggressively. Meanwhile, integrated circuit production and mobile base equipment production decreased by 8.4% and 41.5% month on month respectively in October and as such, both connector strip and lead frame strip production has been extremely sluggish of late. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1100

### **Japan** 

**Doubts over autumn return to pre-quake IP** Japanese industrial production fell by a massive 3.3% month on month in September, the first decrease in IP since the earthquake in March.  Japan had been expected to return to pre-quake levels of output this autumn, but that now seems unlikely, with September’s fall leaving output 7.5% below the February level.  Surveys by the Ministry of the Economy Trade and Industry show that Japanese manufacturers expect to return to growth in October and November, but the strength of the yen and poor demand in Europe are making things tough for exporters.  In addition, the floods in Thailand are causing supply chain disruptions in some industries, such as autos. 

**Wire and cable shipments bounce back** When we wrote last month about the decline in wire and cable shipments in September we cautioned not to read too much into the year-on-year contraction.  Indeed, October shipments have duly bounced back to climb by 3% on the same month a year ago, with the automotive sector continuing its strong recovery, despite weakness in the telecom and power sectors.  Brass mill shipments are performing less well, however, and look set for a mid-single digit full year slide. 

**Autos maintain recovery despite yoy contraction** Japanese vehicle production fell by 4.5% year on year in September, after posting their first gain in August in a year.  However, the move back into negative territory was largely a base effect, as output was very high in September last year due to incentive schemes.  Output continues to recover from the quake and the fourth quarter looks set to be a relatively good one for Japanese vehicle producers, but output for the year is still likely to be down by close to 10%.  The main worry for producers continues to be the yen, with Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association vice chairman Akio Toyoda recently stating that because of the yen “it’s not just a hollowing out, Japan’s production could collapse.”

**Chinese concentrate imports still lag last year’s levels on a cumulative basis** According to Chinese customs data, during October concentrate receipts increased by 10.2%, year on year to 517.1kdmt, bringing the year

to date figure to 5.14Mdmt.  While this is still a reduction on last year’s level (-5.3%) it should be borne in mind that a number of Chinese smelters have been reducing their inventories of concentrates this year and so the consumption of imported material is actually higher than the 2011 import data might imply.  Of the major suppliers, Chile and Kazakhstan have experienced the largest percentage declines in shipments at -22.8% and -30.3% respectively thus far in 2011.  Supply disruptions account for lower shipments from the former while the start up of a new smelter in Kazakhstan probably accounts for the decline in imports from that country.  Overall Chinese concentrate receipts remain on course for ~6.1Mdmt for the year as a whole which would represent a near 6% reduction from the 6.48Mdmt in 2010. 

**Jinchuan orders equipment for its 400kt/a smelter project** Jinchuan’s new primary smelter project moved a step nearer to becoming a reality after the company contracted Finland’s Outotec for the design and delivery of a greenfield copper production plant to be built in the Fangchenggang port area near Bei Hai in Southern China.  According to Outotec the contract value exceeds €30M.  The Finnish company’s scope of delivery includes operating licenses for both Outotec® Flash Smelting and Kennecott-Outotec Flash Converting technologies, basic engineering and delivery of equipment for smelting and converting, anode casting as well as spare parts.  In the first phase, the annual capacity of the smelter will be 400kt/a of cathode copper and it is expected to be commissioned in early 2013.  The project has not received EIS approval, although JInchuan is reportedly confident of obtaining this.  This recent sale to Jinchuan is the third combined Outotec® Flash Smelting and Kennecott-Outotec Flash Converting unit to be sold into China.  In March last year, Tongling Non-Ferrous Metals group spent €15M on a 200kt/a capacity unit (capable of being doubled) to be based in Jinchang, Anhui province, which will be commissioned mid-2012.  The first sale was to Shandong Xiangguang Copper in Yanggu, which started up in late-2007 at an annual capacity rating of 200kt but has since been doubled. When the company announced its intention to construct the project, it mentioned the inclusion of a 200kt/a secondary smelter which is not part of Outotec’s remit and plans for this plant remain unclear. 

**Buyers and sellers around $20/t & 2c/lb apart at the start of the month** Last month we noted the very slow progress in the annual Mating Season negotiations with little in the way of progress to report.  As we then moved into the start of November, trade rumour had it that smelters and miners were broadly $20/t & 2c/lb apart with Japanese buyers talking about numbers of around $70/t & 7c/lb and with various miners looking for a conclusion at around $50/t & 5c/lb.  Such a range in views is nothing unusual at this point in the Mating Season with the gap in terms graduall

y whittled down to a level that becomes acceptable to both parties during subsequent meetings.   Historically, the first settlement has occurred shortly before year end and often during the period between Christmas and New Year.  However, this year has taken many players and market observers by surprise with a whole raft of contracts having been concluded before the end of November. 

**Freeport sets the tone for the Mating Season with numerous settlements during November** It was Freeport who started the ball rolling in this current Mating Season by fixing terms with a Chinese smelter, widely rumoured to be Jiangxi Copper, at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb and a roll over of all other contractual terms.  This deal, which compares with last year’s settlement of $56/t & 5.6c/lb, is thought to include deliveries from both Grasberg and one of the company’s Latin American mines, with around 100kt of concentrates having been priced.  Other Chinese smelting companies including Daye, Jinchuan, Jinlong, Tongling and Shandong Xiangguang apparently then followed suite by agreeing to the same numbers with Freeport.  Since then we hear that the company has struck deals with other customers in India, South Korea and the Philippines.  At the time of writing we are only aware of a fairly small number of contracts outstanding for Freeport, including one in India and several in Japan.  On the one hand these settlement figures are higher than some miners were expecting, but on the flip side of the equation, Japanese buyers will be disappointed with these numbers, as their uplift to a $70/t & 7c/lb objective was key to offsetting the effects of an appreciating yen, lower free metal credits, lower annual cathode premia etc.  Meanwhile, BHP Billiton acting on behalf of Escondida, is thought to be pressing ahead with various alternative pricing structures.  According to trade rumour the company is offering a combination of terms that include an annual portion priced at $50/t & 5c/lb, a Q1 & Q2 2012 portion priced at $40/t & 4c/lb and a Q1 2012 portion priced at $30/t & 3c/lb.  Thus far, we are unaware of any settlements having been concluded using these alternative pricing structures. 

**Does the market have a 2012 benchmark?** And so where does this leave the concentrates market moving forward? We estimate that Freeport has priced around 700kt of concentrates at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb in terms of sales from its Grasberg, Candelaria and Cerro Verde mines and the likelihood is that the company’s remaining contracts will also be finalised at this level.  This is a large tonnage of material fixed at this pricing point but for these TC/RCs to become the benchmark for the 2012 Mating Season, other buyers and sellers will need to accept and adopt them into their contracts. Our feeling is that these TC/RCs will be accepted ‘as is’ by most market players or, alternatively, as has happened in the past, some miners will achieve lower effective settlement terms through pricing at this level bu

**Unrest in Indonesia goes on at Grasberg** There has been very little evident change in the lamentable state of affairs at Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold’s Grasberg operations in Indonesia over the course of this month.  The strike, which began on September 15<sup>th</sup> , is expected to continue through to December 15<sup>th</sup> unless there is a breakthrough as the c.8000 represented labour force continues to hold out for a significant salary raise.  Freeport stated that milling operations had been temporarily suspended since October 22<sup>nd</sup> as repairs were required to the damaged pipeline, and company efforts to effect such repairs were being hampered by road blockages by striking workers, thereby preventing access.  On November 1<sup>st</sup> , Freeport said it would issue an update on the status of operations and provide revised estimates of Q4 production once access is restored and repairs are completed.  As of the 28<sup>th</sup> , no update had been forthcoming.  Grasberg would expect to produce 1400t/d copper and 4.8kozs/d gold in concentrate.  Meanwhile, on a more positive note for Freeport, workers at Cerro Verde have returned to work at the very end of the month, despite no resolution to negotiations with Freeport but instead after receiving guarantees that the regional government would unilaterally draw up a new wage deal. 

**Indonesian unrest briefly extends to PT Newmont** Short-lived strike action was also reported this month at Newmont’s 48.5%-owned Batu Hijau copper-gold mine in Indonesia located in West Sumbawa regency, West Nusa Tenggara.  However, the issue appears to have been resolved after just four days, with no apparent impact on production.  Batu Hijau is expected to produce 120kt copper in concentrate this year.  This will be down by 50% on 2010 due to planned lower mill grades, throughput and recoveries.  The mine-mill has been processing more stockpiled material this year compared to the higher grade Phase 5 ore in 2010 and has completed mill motor replacements giving rise to lower equipment availability.

**Codelco-Anglo relations turn sour** Last month we reported on Codelco’s decision to exercise its option to buy up to 49% of the shares in Anglo American Sur, comprising the Los Bronces and El Soldado mines and Chagres smelter. Codelco was intending to make use of the next “open window” period in which to buy these assets, which is during January 2012.  However, Anglo American responded very swiftly when it announced in mid-November that it had sold a 24.5% stake in Anglo American Sur to Mitsubishi Corp for US$5.4B which, in effect, leaves Codelco being able to buy only half the share that it originally intended.  Anglo’s sale of the 24.5% portion to MC effectively values AAS at c.US$22B on a 100% basis, and represents far better value to Anglo than the US$6.75B that Codelco was likely to pay for its 49% stake in the company.  Codelco believes Anglo’s action violates the agreement that the Chilean parastatal has with Anglo American Sur since it acquired these rights from Enami in 2008.  But Anglo clearly believes that, while Codelco has the right to call upon its option to buy, the agreement does not prevent Anglo from selling as much as 49% of its own stake in AAS.  With Codelco now potentially suing Anglo, the case is now headed for the courts – a process which Codelco CEO Diego Hernandez says could take four years.  Even so, these most recent proceedings are not deterring Anglo from commissioning its US$2.8B expansion at the Los Bronces mine, nor the research into expanding Changres in order to accommodate some of this additional concentrate feed, which would cost a further US$250M.

only access readily available oxide ores and will come to a close with residual leaching.  This is likely to reduce output considerably over the next few years. Golden Grove, located 450km north east of Perth and 280km east of Geraldton port, was operating with a mine life through to 2016 with known copper ore reserves amounting to 1.8Mt.  However, after spending A$22M, MMG will be able to access this new area of 3.3Mt copper ores which will push this deadline out to 2019, and allow a further 59.6kt copper in concentrate production over the three-year period.  Golden Grove also produces c.40-45kt/a zinc contained in concentrate and 4-5kt/a of lead.  MMG is the property’s sixth owner since commissioning in 1990. 

**Latest court ruling at Eagle goes Rio’s way** The latest attempt by opposition groups to halt Rio Tinto subsidiary, Kennecott Eagle Minerals Co (KEMC), from pushing ahead with its Eagle nickel-copper project has failed.  Early this month. KEMC this month heard a decision from the Ingham Circuit Court of Lansing, Michigan that the State Department of Environmental Quality was right to issue environmental permits to KEMC back in 2007.  Groups including the National Wildlife Federation had contended that the proposed underground mine will damage water quality; they will now consider taking their case to the higher Michigan Court of Appeals.  KEMC began blasting works for the underground adit in September this year, and expects to keep Eagle on track to 16kt/a nickel in concentrate and 10kt/a copper in concentrate over a seven- to eight-year mine life from 2013.
